data.body:
# VERDICT: (a) TRUE POSITIVES. All firings are `bound-exceeded`. The drain check is HEALTHY.

AC1 is now satisfied — read directly from `journalctl -u rebar-autodeploy` on
i-00880b2c7f13527c5 via SSM RunShellScript (read-only; no mutation, no config change).

## The reason field behind every firing

    2026-08-07T11:29:23Z  bound-exceeded  in_flight=2  deferred_for=1806s  bound=1800s
    2026-08-07T12:50:04Z  bound-exceeded  in_flight=2  deferred_for=1929s  bound=1800s
    2026-08-12T03:03:04Z  bound-exceeded  in_flight=2  deferred_for=1810s  bound=1800s
    2026-08-12T03:59:33Z  bound-exceeded  in_flight=1  deferred_for=1820s  bound=1800s

**`signal-unavailable` does not appear even once**, in the entire journal back to
2026-07-03. So the branch this ticket correctly flagged as the alarming reading — "the
/health in_flight probe is inert and every deploy has been running blind, a silent
regression of 34cd" — is **ruled out**. AC2 is not applicable; the probe works.

The ticket's circumstantial inference from the deferral run-up was right.

## There is a FOURTH firing this ticket does not list

`2026-08-12T03:59:33Z` (= 2026-08-11 20:59 PDT). The sweep window closed at
2026-08-12T04:00Z and this landed 27 seconds inside it, so it was missed. It is
**4 firings in 7 days**, not 3 — and the 4th came ~56 minutes after the 3rd, i.e. a
second full 1800s bound was spent back-to-back with the first.

## Metric-artifact false positive: checked and EXCLUDED

Worth recording since it was the leading alternative hypothesis. `observability.sh`
§4e counts markers by grepping the WHOLE unit journal cumulatively and publishing
`total - prev`, with `[ "$new" -lt 0 ] && new=$total`. If journald ever vacuumed the
unit's history, `total` would drop below the stored offset and that guard would
re-publish the entire remaining count as "new this interval" — spuriously re-firing a
1-datapoint, threshold-`>0` alarm on history that had already been counted.

Measured on the box: journal total = **7**, offset file
`/var/lib/rebar/autodeploy-interrupt-offset` = **7**, and the unit journal still
reaches back to 2026-07-03T19:50:40Z. No rotation has occurred, offset and total agree
exactly, and every CloudWatch datapoint has a matching journal line at the same minute
(3 on 08-03 pre-fix, 4 post-fix). **No double-count. Every firing is a real, distinct
interrupt.** (The latent rotation hazard is real but has not triggered; filing it
separately rather than conflating it with this ticket.)

## ROOT CAUSE: the bound's rationale assumes serial reviews; the bot runs CONCURRENT ones

This is the part that upgrades the finding from "the bot is busy" to "34cd's bound
argument does not hold". The full deferral episode preceding the 03:03:04 interrupt,
one line per ~2.1-minute tick, unbroken:

    02:32:54  in_flight=2  deferred_for=0s      <- episode opens
    02:35:03  in_flight=2  129s
    02:37:14  in_flight=2  260s
    02:39:24  in_flight=2  390s
    02:41:33  in_flight=2  519s
    02:43:43  in_flight=2  649s
    02:45:54  in_flight=2  780s
    02:48:03  in_flight=1  909s
    02:50:14  in_flight=1  1040s
    02:52:24  in_flight=1  1169s
    02:54:33  in_flight=2  1299s   <- climbs back to 2
    02:56:34  in_flight=2  1420s
    02:58:43  in_flight=2  1549s
    03:00:53  in_flight=2  1679s
    03:03:04  in_flight=2  1810s   -> AUTODEPLOY_REVIEW_INTERRUPT

Every tick deferred; the episode never reset, so the gate behaved exactly as designed.
But look at `in_flight`: it oscillates 2 -> 1 -> 2 and **never reaches 0** across 30
continuous minutes.

34cd justified `DEPLOY_DEFER_MAX=1800` like this (quoting its own implementation note):

> the bot wraps every review in `asyncio.wait_for(..., REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS)` on both
> paths (default 1200s), so no single review can outlive that and **in_flight
> necessarily reaches 0 within it**. 1800s is 1.5x that ceiling [...] so the bound is
> only reachable by a CHRONICALLY busy bot, never by one ordinary review.

The premise is true per-review and false in aggregate. `REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` bounds
each review's lifetime, but `in_flight` is a **concurrent gauge**: with two reviews
overlapping and new ones arriving as old ones finish, the counter is refilled before it
can drain, so the idle window the bound waits for never opens. No review outlived 1200s
here — the trace shows completions (2->1) throughout. The bound is not being defeated by
a stuck review; it is being outlasted by ordinary pipelining.

So "reachable only by a chronically busy bot" is accurate as written, but the implied
rarity does not follow: **any landing burst that sustains >=1 concurrent review for 30
minutes spends the bound**, and at present cadence that is roughly weekly, twice in one
hour on 2026-08-11. The exceptional case has become routine because the reasoning
treated a concurrency gauge as if it were a single-review timer.

## STOPPING HERE — the remedy is an operator decision, not a behavior-preserving fix

Per the bug-bash brief I stop at diagnosis when the fix would change autodeploy or
review behavior. Every candidate does:

- **Raise `DEPLOY_DEFER_MAX`.** Trades a killed review for a longer deploy stall, and
  34cd deliberately pinned it to 1.5x `REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` with a test asserting
  `bound >= REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`. Note the trace shows raising it alone may not even
  work: the episode was saturated, so a larger bound just defers the same kill. This
  ticket was right to flag it as the wrong reflex.
- **Cap review concurrency**, so `in_flight` can actually reach 0. Changes review
  throughput.
- **Accept it** (AC3) and treat interrupts as ordinary burst residue — which then argues
  the alarm should not be a 1-datapoint pager.

My recommendation, for whoever takes the decision: this is **not an outage** — the
reconciler retries each killed review, and no `signal-unavailable` means the drain check
is doing its job on every other tick. But the alarm is currently paging on a condition
that is now normal-cadence, so the real choice is between accepting the interrupts and
retuning the alarm, versus making `in_flight` drainable. I would not raise the bound.

## AC4 remains genuinely open and is the one cheap, low-risk piece

`rebar/host:review_interrupts` is dimensionless, which is why this ticket had to hedge
between two readings with opposite fixes and why confirming it needed host shell access
at all. Splitting the two reasons into distinct countable tokens/metrics (or adding a
reason dimension) would let a future sweep read the answer straight from CloudWatch.
That is observability-only and does not touch deploy or review behavior — but it is a
Terraform alarm-contract change requiring an apply, so I am leaving it for the operator
to sequence with whatever AC3 decides, rather than landing it ahead of that decision.

## Method note

Read-only throughout: `aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics`, and SSM RunShellScript
issuing only `journalctl`/`cat`/`grep`. Nothing on the box or in AWS was modified, and
no code was changed.
